A.explanation: This is the power in the wires, about $0.44\text{ W}$, but it has not been multiplied by the time of $3600\text{ s}$ to get energy.

B.explanation: This assumes the full $12\text{ V}$ is across the $4.9\,\Omega$ wires to give about $29\text{ W}$ and then uses $t = 1\text{ s}$ instead of $1.0\text{ hour} = 3600\text{ s}$.

C.explanation: The current of $0.30\text{ A}$ in the $4.9\,\Omega$ wires gives about $0.44\text{ W}$, which over $3600\text{ s}$ is about $1.6\text{ kJ}$ of thermal energy.

D.explanation: This is close to the total output energy $3.6\text{ W} \times 3600\text{ s}$ minus the wire loss, so it is the energy to the component, not the energy dissipated in the wires.

hints: First find the current in the series circuit from the supply output: $P = VI$ with $P = 3.6\text{ W}$ and $V = 12\text{ V}$.
That same current flows in the $4.9\,\Omega$ connecting wires, so the wire heating power is $P = I^2R$, not $V^2/R$ with $12\text{ V}$.
Convert $1.0\text{ hour}$ to $3600\text{ s}$ and use $E = Pt$ for the thermal energy in the wires.
walkthrough: Find the circuit current from the power supply output. Using $P = VI$, $I = P/V = 3.6/12 = 0.30\text{ A}$. This current flows through both the wires and the component.
Find the power dissipated in the connecting wires. The wires have $R = 4.9\,\Omega$, so $P_{wire} = I^2R = (0.30)^2 \times 4.9$.
Calculate $P_{wire} = 0.09 \times 4.9 = 0.441\text{ W}$. Do not use $12\text{ V}$ across the wires because most of the $12\text{ V}$ is across the component.
Convert the heating time to seconds: $t = 1.0\text{ hour} = 3600\text{ s}$.
Calculate thermal energy: $E = P_{wire}t = 0.441 \times 3600 \approx 1590\text{ J} \approx 1.6\text{ kJ}$. This is option C.
